We spent the last quarter rebuilding how the support team handles refunds. The old process had four approval steps, two spreadsheets, and a Slack channel nobody read. Refunds under fifty dollars now get approved automatically, and anything above that goes to one person instead of three. The queue that used to sit at two days is under four hours. We also changed the language in the refund email. It used to open with a paragraph about our policy; now it opens with the amount and the date the money lands. Complaints about the email dropped by half in the first month. The part that surprised me was the reporting. Once the approvals lived in one place, the finance team could see refund reasons for the first time, and the biggest category was not product defects but shipping delays from one carrier. We moved forty percent of that volume to a second carrier in June. Two things did not work. The automatic approvals caught a handful of duplicate requests that a human would have noticed, so we added a check for repeat orders within thirty days. And the new email confused customers who had paid with store credit, because the money does not land anywhere; we now send a different version to those customers. We also learned something about staffing. The support lead had assumed the refund queue was a two-person job, and it was, but only because two people were doing the same work twice. With the approvals consolidated, one of them moved to the exchanges desk and the other picked up the carrier escalations, which had been sitting with nobody in particular. Neither of them wanted to go back. The numbers for the quarter: refund volume flat at about nine hundred a month, average time to money down from fifty-one hours to three and a half, email complaints down from around sixty a month to twenty-eight, and the duplicate-request check has caught nineteen cases since we added it. The carrier change cost us about four percent on shipping for that segment and saved us more than that in refunds. Next quarter we are looking at exchanges, which still run through the old process. If the refund changes hold, exchanges should be simpler, since most of them are really refunds plus a new order. I will post the numbers when we have a full quarter of data.
